answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most options before any memory is consulted. Rollback is ruled out by compliance regardless of how well memory_b1 worked on day 18. Regional failover (memory_b2) does not help here: the suspect release is presumably deployed in all regions, so the degradation likely follows the traffic, and shifting a write-heavy path at settlement peak is the single highest-risk way to lose in-flight customer writes \ the one thing the primary objective forbids. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) contained a *partner dependency* outage by failing fast; here the failure is internal write-path saturation, and failing fast on our own writes sheds exactly the transactions we must not drop. Adding capacity (memory_b3) worked when it was *provisioned ahead* of a known peak; we are 90 minutes into the peak, and provisioning latency plus warm-up probably lands after the window closes. That leaves read-replica routing (memory_b5) as the only lever that plausibly relieves primary contention without reverting the patch and without touching the write path itself. I want to verify memory_b5 specifically because the consolidated summary asserts a causal story ('write latency recovered the same day') that is exactly the kind of claim that gets tidied up in consolidation \ 'same day' is loose enough to be coincidence, and I need the original record to know whether the day-55 primary was actually read-contended and whether that resembles a settlement-peak write burst. If the archive shows read load was incidental on day 55, the analogy collapses and add_capacity becomes the better bet despite the timing. Scale is deliberately small and guarded: shift only report/dashboard query classes first, hold transactional and reconciliation reads on the primary, and watch write p99 for a clear signal before widening. Downstream value risk is real and I am flagging it \ replica lag means any settlement, balance, or reconciliation logic that silently reads a routed replica could act on stale state and produce financially wrong outcomes that look like successful writes; that is worse than latency, so those query classes stay pinned. I am not treating this as a solved problem: the underlying cause may be the unrevertable patch itself (new write amplification, added crypto or audit work per transaction), in which case read routing buys headroom but does not fix it, and the next window needs a forward-fix or targeted capacity rather than a repeat of this lever.
